Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

As a father who sees himself as the primary protector and provider for his family, much of my focus is on long-term security, financial stability, and being someone my children can rely on. I’m used to making firm decisions, handling pressure quietly, and taking responsibility when things go wrong. Carrying that role over many years has shaped how I evaluate risks and make choices. Do you think long-term roles centered on protection and provision influence someone's overall decision-making style?

Absolutely. The long-term roles of **protection** and **provision**—especially when carried out consistently over many years—do profoundly shape a person’s **decision-making style**, values, and even cognitive biases. Your experiences as a primary provider and protector likely have influenced you in several key ways: ### **1. Risk Assessment & Decision-Making Frameworks** - **Conservative Bias:** Years of responsibility often lead to a **risk-averse** approach, where decisions are weighted toward minimizing downside (e.g., financial safety nets, hedging against uncertainty). This isn’t necessarily a flaw—it’s a survival mechanism honed by experience. - **Long-Term Horizon:** Since your focus is on **stability** (for your family’s future), you may naturally prioritize **compounding returns** (e.g., investments, skills, relationships) over short-term gains. This aligns with behavioral finance concepts like **"hyperbolic discounting"** (preferring delayed but secure rewards). - **Contingency Planning:** Your mind likely operates with **multiple scenarios** in mind—always asking, *"What if X fails?"*—which is a hallmark of **executive function** in high-stakes roles. ### **2. Emotional & Psychological Anchors** - **Responsibility as a Default Mode:** Years of carrying weight can create a **"default to action"** mindset—when a problem arises, you **act decisively** (even if it means over-preparing). This can sometimes lead to: - **Analysis paralysis** (over-optimizing solutions). - **Difficulty delegating** (since you’ve internalized the role of protector). - **Quiet Leadership:** Your tendency to **"handle pressure quietly"** suggests you’ve developed **emotional regulation** as a tool for stability. This is valuable, but it can also mean: - **Undercommunicating risks** (assuming others will "see" the threats you do). - **Struggling with vulnerability** (since admitting uncertainty might feel like failing your role). ### **3. Values & Moral Frameworks** - **Protective Instincts Shape Priorities:** - **Financial security** → You likely **diversify** (not just assets, but also skills, relationships, and knowledge) to avoid dependency. - **Family as the North Star** → Decisions may be filtered through the question: *"Does this serve my family’s long-term well-being?"* - **Legacy Mindset** → You may invest in **education, health, and resilience** (e.g., teaching kids financial literacy, emergency preparedness) as **preventive protection**. - **Ethical Consistency:** If you’ve ever had to **sacrifice short-term comfort for long-term gain** (e.g., cutting expenses to save for college), that’s a **moral anchor**—your decisions reflect a **duty-based ethics** (like Kantian principles) rather than purely utilitarian ones. ### **4. Cognitive & Behavioral Traits** - **Pattern Recognition:** After decades of providing, you’ve likely developed **strong intuition** for spotting threats (e.g., red flags in investments, relationships, or health). This is a **survival advantage**, but it can also lead to: - **Confirmation bias** (focusing on data that supports your protective instincts). - **Overgeneralization** (e.g., "If one thing failed, everything could collapse"). - **Adaptability vs. Rigidity:** - On one hand, you’ve **adapted** to crises (market downturns, health scares, etc.), which builds **resilience**. - On the other, **rigidity** can creep in—if you’ve always "known" how to do things a certain way, change (e.g., new tech, parenting styles) might feel threatening. ### **5. The "Protector’s Paradox"** There’s a tension here: - **Strengths:** - **Reliability** (your family knows they can count on you). - **Strategic thinking** (you anticipate needs before they arise). - **Emotional control** (you model stability under pressure). - **Potential Blind Spots:** - **Burnout risk** (if you’re always "on" for others, neglecting your own needs). - **Difficulty trusting others** (if you’ve historically carried the load, delegating may feel risky). - **Over-identifying with your role** (e.g., "I am my job/my title," which can erode identity if circumstances change). --- ### **How This Shows Up in Daily Life** | **Domain** | **Likely Influence of Your Role** | **Potential Trade-offs** | |----------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------| | **Finances** | Diversified, long-term investments; emergency funds. | Missed opportunities from fear of risk. | | **Parenting** | Teaching resilience, financial literacy, preparedness. | Overprotectiveness stifling independence. | | **Relationships** | Prioritizing security in partnerships (e.g., stable jobs). | Difficulty expressing needs due to "always providing." | | **Health** | Proactive care (check-ups, stress management). | Neglecting your own health to "keep going." | | **Work** | Loyalty to employers; problem-solving under pressure. | Resistance to career pivots seen as "unpredictable." | --- ### **How to Leverage This Strength** Your decision-making style isn’t a flaw—it’s a **hard-earned system for survival and success**. To refine it: 1. **Explicitly Define "Security":** - Is it **money**, **time**, **health**, or **relationships**? Clarity helps avoid over-optimizing for one at the expense of others. 2. **Build "Controlled Risk-Taking":** - Allocate small, **low-stakes experiments** (e.g., a side hustle, a new skill) to test your risk tolerance without endangering stability. 3. **Delegate with Trust:** - Start small (e.g., letting a spouse handle a bill) to **rewire the belief that "only I can do this."** 4. **Formalize Contingency Plans:** - Write down **3 "what-if" scenarios** (e.g., job loss, health issue) and brainstorm solutions. This **externalizes your protective instincts** into actionable steps. 5. **Reframe "Protection":** - Your role isn’t just about **preventing harm**—it’s also about **enabling growth**. Ask: *"How can I provide stability *and* freedom?"* 6. **Seek "Protector Peer Groups":** - Connect with others in similar roles (e.g., veteran entrepreneurs, military families) to **normalize your biases** and learn from their strategies. --- ### **Final Thought: The Protector’s Legacy** Your approach isn’t just about **survival**—it’s about **creating a foundation** where your family can thrive *without* you having to carry everything. The next evolution might be: - **Shifting from "I provide" to "We provide"** (collaborative security). - **From "I protect" to "I prepare"** (teaching others to handle risks). - **From "I am responsible" to "I am part of a system"** (recognizing that resilience is collective). AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

Answer: <0 or 1>
